prompt.context: A cable TV company from Canada, World View, had recently entered the US market in the northeast to expand its market share. World View saw this move as an opportunity to capture a large part of the US market (4MM consumers) in a market with very little competition.
prompt.question: However, in the last couple of years, much to the surprise of management, World View has been unable to make a profit. You have been hired to figure out why and advise them on their next move.

clarifying_info.q: Did World View incur additional costs per customer in the new US market?
clarifying_info.a: No. Based on the potential number of subscribers, they have instituted the same system that was in place in Canada. Costs associated with cable wire, debt, and maintenance are all proportionally the same.

clarifying_info.q: How many of the 4MM potential customers have signed up?
Are other cable companies capturing the remaining market?
clarifying_info.a: No, competition from other cable companies is not an issue. Those who have not subscribed simply do not have cable.

clarifying_info.q: How is the consumer in the northeast US different from the Canadian consumer in terms of viewing behavior?
clarifying_info.a: The Canadian consumer does not rely much on local stations — cable is a major source of entertainment and news. In the northeast US, consumers tend to shy away from paying the $40 per month and settle for watching local stations.

clarifying_info.q: Does the northeast US market have a lower income level?
How many local stations are there, and do they meet consumer needs?
clarifying_info.a: There are about 16 local stations with coverage over the entire northeast. They provide programming that consumers want, and the average consumer in the northeast watches regular TV more than cable compared to the Canadian consumer.

clarifying_info.q: How is the reception of local stations, and how much do they charge?
clarifying_info.a: They have very good reception and are part of basic TV, so they are free.

clarifying_info.q: Is World View providing programming that local stations are not?
clarifying_info.a: Some, but consumers don't seem interested. They don't feel it is worth $40.

framework: Apply the profitability framework: analyze both revenue and cost sides of the problem.
On the revenue side, examine the number of subscribers and pricing relative to the total addressable market.
On the cost side, check whether per-customer costs differ between Canada and the US northeast.
Analyze consumer differences: viewing habits, income levels, and willingness to pay between the Canadian and US northeast markets.
Assess the competitive landscape including substitutes, not just direct cable competitors.

questions.prompt: Why is World View unable to make a profit despite low cable competition?
questions.guidance: Costs are proportionally the same as Canada, so the problem lies on the revenue side. Only 2.1MM of 4MM potential customers have subscribed — a 52.5% penetration rate. The root cause is not other cable companies but free local TV stations acting as substitutes. The northeast consumer has lower income (20% below Canada average) and strong free alternatives (16 local stations, good reception, no cost), making the $40/month cable price unattractive. Consumer behavior and willingness to pay differ fundamentally from Canada.

math.setup: Subscriber penetration rate: actual subscribers / potential market
math.answer: 52.5% — nearly half the market is not subscribing

questions.prompt: What is the competitive landscape that explains the low subscriber rate?
questions.guidance: The true competition is free-to-air local television, not other cable providers. 16 local stations cover the entire northeast, have good reception, and are free. Consumers with lower incomes (20% below Canadian average) rationally choose free TV over $40/month cable. This is a substitute-driven problem, not a direct competitor problem.

brainstorming.prompt: What strategic options does World View have to turn around its US northeast operations?

categories.name: Pricing & Packaging
ideas: Offer a smaller, cheaper cable package targeting consumers who want only a few channels beyond basic
Introduce tiered pricing (e.g., $15–$20 entry tier) to convert non-subscribers price-sensitive consumers
Bundle internet or phone services to increase perceived value

categories.name: Content & Value Proposition
ideas: Identify and invest in programming that local stations cannot provide (sports, premium movies, international content)
Educate consumers on the incremental value of cable beyond local stations
Promote exclusive or on-demand content to differentiate from free TV

categories.name: Geographic Focus
ideas: Scale back operations to a specific sub-region with higher income levels or weaker local TV coverage
Focus on urban areas with higher WTP and income

categories.name: Exit / Restructure
ideas: If no strategy achieves profitability, exit the US northeast market
Consider selling or leasing infrastructure to another operator
Re-evaluate entry into US markets with different consumer profiles (e.g., regions with fewer/worse local stations)

recommendation: World View should first attempt to re-price its offering with a lower-cost entry package (targeting the income gap and free-TV competition) and sharpen its content differentiation to give consumers a compelling reason to pay.
If pricing and content changes do not improve subscriber penetration within a defined period, World View should scale back to the most profitable sub-regions or exit the northeast US market entirely.
risks: A lower-priced package may cannibalize revenue from existing 2.1MM subscribers if not structured carefully
Content investment to differentiate from local stations requires additional cost and may not shift consumer behavior quickly
Exiting the market means writing off sunk infrastructure costs
next_steps: Pilot a lower-cost cable tier in one metro area to test price elasticity
Survey current non-subscribers to identify the minimum value proposition needed to convert them
Conduct a full P&L analysis of each sub-region to identify where contribution margin is positive
Set a 12-month profitability threshold; if not met, initiate market exit planning
